Obsession in literature describes the psychological state in which a character becomes consumed by a single desire, compulsion, or belief to the exclusion of all other reality. Russian fiction, particularly the work of Dostoevsky and Pushkin, made obsession a central theme, exploring how fixation destroys the self and leads inexorably toward tragedy. Obsession reveals the fragility of reason and the terrible power of human will.

Obsession is distinct from passion in that it involves the replacement of authentic will with compulsive repetition. The subject cannot choose to stop. Dostoevsky's The Gambler traces the protagonist's descent into gambling addiction, where the act of betting becomes psychologically identical with existence itself. The gambler becomes unmade by his obsession. Pushkin's The Queen of Spades centers on Hermann's obsession with a supernatural secret to guarantee wealth, demonstrating how obsession feeds on superstition and produces madness. The obsessed character hallucinates.

Russian psychological fiction uses obsession to interrogate the limits of reason and morality. The obsessed character becomes a test case for how the self dissolves under compulsion. Obsession often masks deeper psychological needs—for control, for meaning, for escape—making it both a symptom and a disease. It is always a failure of the authentic self. Literary obsession often spirals into violence, madness, or death, serving as a moral mirror for the destructive potential within human consciousness. The obsessed character's trajectory is tragic.

Melville's Moby Dick presents obsession as a philosophical stance. Ahab's pursuit of the whale becomes a meditation on will, fate, and the refusal to accept limitation. Modern literature and psychology converge on obsession as a model of damaged consciousness. Obsessive-compulsive disorder, addiction, and erotic fixation become subjects through which writers explore compulsion and agency. Through Dostoevsky's novella about obsessive gambling and the disappearance of selfhood, and Pushkin's exploration of supernatural obsession and superstitious madness, we see how obsession became central to how writers interrogate the limits of the self.
